title: Karnataka launches five-year plan to tackle antibiotic resistance
summary: The Karnataka State Action Plan for Containment of Antimicrobial Resistance (K-SAPCAR) 2026-2030 was unveiled at a state-level workshop in the city Thursday.

Bengaluru: With bacteria increasingly becoming resistant to commonly used antibiotics, the state govt has launched a five-year action plan to contain antimicrobial resistance (AMR), proposing stricter curbs on over-the-counter antibiotic sales, prescription audits in hospitals and surveillance of antibiotic use in livestock and food production.The Karnataka State Action Plan for Containment of Antimicrobial Resistance (K-SAPCAR) 2026-2030 was unveiled at a state-level workshop in the city Thursday.

The scale of the problem is evident from the Karnataka AMR Surveillance Network Annual Report 2025, cited in the action plan. It found that nearly three out of four samples of Gram-negative bacteria tested were resistant to ceftriaxone, an antibiotic commonly used to treat infections. Similarly, nearly three out of four samples of Gram-positive bacteria showed resistance to ciprofloxacin. Gram-positive and Gram-negative are two broad groups of bacteria, classified based on differences in their cell walls, with both groups including bacteria that can cause infections in humans.

Advt

Among the key proposals is stricter enforcement of the prohibition on selling antibiotics without valid prescriptions. The plan also calls for mandatory mention of the prescribing doctor’s registration number on prescriptions, monitoring of Schedule H1 drug sales and periodic prescription audits in both public and private healthcare facilities.It proposes establishing antimicrobial stewardship programmes in all hospitals, including private facilities, to ensure rational antibiotic use. Hospitals will also be encouraged to publish antibiograms — reports showing which antibiotics are effective against bacteria identified in their facilities — every six months or annually. Reserve-category antibiotics are proposed to be restricted to specified indications, with prior authorisation under hospital stewardship programmes.

The plan also extends surveillance beyond human healthcare. It proposes regular testing of meat and egg samples for antibiotic residues, regulation of antibiotics used in animal feed for growth promotion and disease prevention, and monitoring of critically important antibiotics used in food-animal farming.Strengthening laboratory infrastructure, implementing information management systems across public health facilities and developing a state-level surveillance network involving public and private institutions are among the other priorities.

The plan adopts a ‘one health’ approach, bringing together human, animal and environmental health departments. It also proposes monitoring antibiotic residues in sewage, water, soil and pharmaceutical waste.

Advt

Dr Rajini M, director of the health department, highlighted the need for rational antimicrobial use, stronger laboratory and surveillance systems and coordinated action across sectors.
